record_identity.title: Nx s1ngularity malware weaponized local AI coding CLIs during credential-harvesting supply-chain attack

incident_identity.date_basis: Nx states that malicious package versions were published on 26 August 2025 and active for approximately four hours. GitGuardian documents follow-on abuse of stolen GitHub tokens on 28 August 2025 to make private repositories public. The range bounds the directly evidenced initial and follow-on phases reviewed here.

summary: Attackers stole an Nx npm publishing token through a GitHub Actions injection flaw and published malicious Nx package versions on 26 August 2025. The package post-install malware directly harvested credentials and sensitive files and also attempted to invoke locally configured Claude, Gemini and Amazon Q command-line tools with prompts designed to identify additional sensitive files for exfiltration. Results and stolen credentials were uploaded to public GitHub repositories. GitGuardian identified 2,349 distinct secrets in 1,079 affected repositories during the initial phase, with more than 1,100 still valid at the time of analysis, and later observed 10,767 private repositories made public, exposing 82,901 secrets including 11,168 then-valid secrets. The AI-assisted path was only one component of the attack: GitGuardian reported that only 95 of 366 targeted systems produced the requested AI-generated inventory file, and Wiz separately found substantial refusal, configuration and workspace-restriction failure rates across the invoked AI tools.

vigil_assessment.factual_basis: Nx directly confirms that malicious packages attempted to use local AI tools including Claude and Gemini while scanning user systems and uploading results to public GitHub repositories. GitGuardian's analysis quantifies credential and repository exposure and reports that 95 of 366 systems where LLM tools were targeted produced the requested inventory file. Wiz independently describes the malware invoking Claude, Gemini and Amazon Q with permissive command-line flags and prompt-engineering attempts, while documenting substantial refusals and execution failures. OECD.AI later indexed the s1ngularity campaign as an AI incident, but its entry is used only as discovery and registry corroboration rather than primary technical evidence.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: Malicious code already running on developer systems discovered locally installed AI coding agents and tried to repurpose them for reconnaissance and file enumeration. The evidence does not show that those tools caused the initial Nx compromise, and most observed invocations did not produce the requested inventory. Because the tools, configurations and outcomes were heterogeneous, the record does not attribute one common internal failure mechanism to them.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: The incident demonstrates a distinct agent-security surface: malware can discover and invoke trusted local AI developer tools, attempt to bypass their permission and safety boundaries, and use successful sessions to extend reconnaissance beyond static malware logic. It also shows why outcome assessment must preserve partial refusal and failure rates rather than treating all targeted AI tools as uniformly compliant.
assessment_boundaries: The malware directly harvested credentials and files independently of AI-tool assistance; the full incident impact must not be attributed to the AI tools.

GitGuardian observed only 95 successful requested inventory-file writes among 366 systems where LLM tools were targeted, and Wiz reports additional refusals, configuration failures and workspace restrictions.
The exact underlying model versions serving Claude, Gemini and Amazon Q CLI interactions are not established in the reviewed evidence.
The reviewed public evidence does not establish how many exposed secrets were subsequently abused beyond the documented follow-on repository-publication phase.
The OECD.AI entry is AI-generated registry material and is not treated as primary evidence for technical attribution or quantitative impact.

taxonomy_classification.classification_basis: The occurrence establishes malicious invocation of heterogeneous AI coding agents as part of a real credential-harvesting campaign, but the public evidence does not support one current selectable VIGIL system-failure mechanism across all affected tools. Successful and refused interactions coexist, exact runtime states are unavailable, and malicious external invocation alone is not converted into a Failure Class.
